title: From Lesson to Unit

pts: A single lesson teaches a discrete point; a unit builds toward a larger communicative outcome across several classes.
Learners need repeated, varied encounters with target language before it becomes reliably usable — one lesson rarely provides enough.
Planning at the unit level forces coherence that planning lesson-by-lesson can quietly lose.

v: One textbook unit (four to six lessons)

items: Read the whole textbook unit before teaching any of it.
List what each lesson teaches (vocabulary, grammar, skill).
Ask: what could learners do at the end of the unit that they could not do at the start? Write it in one sentence.
If the answer is unclear, the unit may be a collection of lessons rather than a sequence. Note where connections are missing.
Plan one small change per lesson that links it to the end goal.
Compare two consecutive textbook units: does the second build on the first?
Do this activity with a colleague who teaches the same grade.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A textbook unit read as a collection and as a sequence:

lines: Collection: L1 food vocabulary; L2 countable/uncountable nouns; L3 reading about a festival meal; L4 writing a recipe.
Sequence: all four lessons feed one end goal, Learners can explain how to make a favourite dish to a visitor.

blocks.x: Links added: L1 includes words for ingredients in learners’ own dishes; L2 practises some and any with those ingredients; L3 notes sequencing words; L4 becomes the final task.

body: Figure 11.1 A pile of lessons and a staircase

Purpose: to contrast a collection with a sequence. Content: on the left, four lesson blocks piled loosely, labelled L1–L4, with no clear top. On the right, the same four blocks arranged as a staircase leading to a flag labelled ‘Unit goal’. Style: simple 3D blocks, two colours. Board version: four boxes, then a staircase.

items: Google Docs (free). A one-page unit overview template: goal, lessons, links.

blocks.x: A single sheet at the front of the textbook unit with the goal written at the top.

pts: Revisit target language across a unit with increasing complexity, rather than teaching it once and leaving it behind.
Each pass through the spiral adds a layer — new context, more precision, freer use — rather than simple repetition.
This is recycling (Unit 5) scaled up from vocabulary items to whole language points.

items: Choose one language point (for example, talking about the future).
Search the contents page for every place it appears.
Draw a spiral: each turn is an appearance, labelled with the unit and what is new each time.
Look for gaps: long stretches with no return, or repeats with nothing new.
Plan short returns (a warmer, a speaking task) to fill the gaps.
Make spiral maps for vocabulary sets (family, food, travel).
Ask learners to find where a language point returns in their book.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A spiral for future forms across a school year:

lines: Turn 1 (Unit 2, A1): I’m going to visit my aunt. (plans)
Turn 2 (Unit 5, A2): It’s going to rain. (predictions from evidence)
Turn 3 (Unit 8, A2): I’m meeting Ravi at six. (arrangements)
Turn 4 (Unit 11, B1): I think I’ll… / I’m going to… (decisions and plans contrasted)

body: Purpose: to show spiral sequencing. Content: a coiled spiral rising from bottom to top, with four points marked on successive turns. Each point has a small label card with the unit number and an example sentence. The spiral widens slightly as it rises, suggesting increasing complexity. Style: clean, one colour gradient. Board version: a coil drawn with four dots.

items: Google Sheets (free). A row per language point and a column per unit; tick where it appears, and colour the cells to show gaps.

blocks.x: A large sheet of chart paper with the spiral drawn for the most important language point of the year.

body: Bruner’s spiral curriculum (1960) was proposed for school subjects in general, not for languages. Language teachers adopted it readily because language learning is already spiral by nature: no one learns the past tense once and for all.

pts: Every unit needs one overarching can-do outcome that individual lesson aims feed into, not just a shared topic.
Write the unit aim before sequencing lessons — sequencing without it produces a pile of related activities, not a build.
Check each lesson's aim against the unit aim: does this lesson move learners measurably closer to it?

items: Write one can-do statement for the whole unit.
List the lesson aims underneath.
For each lesson aim, write one line: ‘This moves learners closer to the unit aim because…’
If you cannot write the line, change or cut that lesson.
Share the unit aim with learners on the first day of the unit.
Write the unit aim with learners, choosing from two or three options.
Display the unit aim on a wall chart and tick lessons as they are completed.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A unit aim with its lessons:

lines: Unit aim: Learners can plan a class picnic and present the plan to the headteacher.
L1 Vocabulary for food, places and transport → needed to discuss options.
L2 Suggestions and agreeing (Why don’t we…?) → needed for planning.
L3 Going to for plans → needed to describe the plan.
L4 Reading a sample plan → model for the final product.
L5 Planning and presenting → the cumulative task.

body: Purpose: to show lesson aims supporting a unit aim. Content: a simple house. The roof carries the unit aim. Five pillars beneath it carry the lesson aims. The floor is labelled ‘what learners already know’. Style: clean line drawing. Board version: a triangle roof on five lines.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers). Make a unit-aim poster for the classroom.

blocks.x: The unit aim written in a corner of the board for every lesson in the unit.

points.sub: No single skill carries it all
pts: Distribute listening, speaking, reading and writing across the unit so none is left out or over-relied on.
A common failure mode is a unit that is accidentally all reading and grammar, with speaking added only as an afterthought.
Map skills against lessons early in planning, not after the fact.

items: For each lesson in the unit, list the main activities.
Colour each activity by skill: listening, speaking, reading, writing.
Count the minutes per skill across the unit.
If one skill dominates or is missing, change one activity per lesson to rebalance.
Record the final balance in the unit plan.
Add systems (grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation) as further colours.
Compare the balance with the needs identified in Unit 2.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An unbalanced unit and a fix:

lines: Before: reading 45 minutes, grammar exercises 60 minutes, writing 30 minutes, listening 5 minutes, speaking 10 minutes.
After: reading 35, grammar 35, writing 30, listening 25, speaking 45. (Speaking and listening added through a pair task and a teacher-read model.)

blocks.x: The balance need not be equal; it should match learners’ needs.

body: Purpose: to visualize skills distribution. Content: two horizontal stacked bars, ‘Before’ and ‘After’, each divided into coloured segments for listening, speaking, reading, writing and systems. Before is dominated by two colours; after is more even. A small legend. Style: clean chart without exact numbers on the bars. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Sheets (free). A simple table with minutes per skill per lesson and an automatic stacked bar chart.

blocks.x: Coloured pencils on a paper plan.

pts: End the unit with a task that requires everything taught across it, not just the final lesson's content.
This task functions as the unit's real assessment — a natural, communicative check of what has actually transferred.
Design the cumulative task first, then plan backward through the unit toward it.

v: 60 minutes (the final lesson of a unit)

items: Remind learners of the unit aim.
In groups of four, learners plan a class picnic within a budget: place, transport, food, activities, timings.
Groups prepare a two-minute presentation using the language from earlier lessons.
Each group presents to the ‘headteacher’ (the teacher or a visiting colleague), who asks one question.
The class votes for the best plan.
Learners self-assess against the unit aim.
Make it written: a short plan to be displayed on the notice board.
Invite a real headteacher or another class as audience.
Support: provide a planning grid with prompts.
Stretch: groups must justify one choice with a comparison (cheaper than, closer than).

lines: We’re going to go to ______. We’re going to travel by ______ because ______. We’re going to take ______. First we’ll ______, then ______. It will cost ______.

blocks.x: Checklist for the ‘headteacher’: Was the plan clear? Did the group use suggestion language during planning? Did they use going to for the plan? Did everyone speak?

body: Figure 11.5 The cumulative task at the top of the unit

Purpose: to show the task as the destination. Content: the staircase from Figure 11.1 with the final step replaced by a stage and small figures presenting to an audience. Labels on earlier steps show the language each lesson contributed. Style: consistent with Figure 11.1. Board version: not applicable.

items: Canva for Education or Google Slides (free). Groups prepare a one-slide visual for their plan.

blocks.x: A poster on chart paper for each group.

body: Write the cumulative task first, before planning any lesson in the unit. Then ask of every lesson: what does this give learners for the final task? This single question removes more wasted activity than any other planning technique.

pts: Deliberately reintroduce earlier lessons' vocabulary and grammar mid-unit, not only within the lesson that first taught them.
A five-minute warmer recycling last lesson's language costs little and pays back significantly in retention.
This extends Unit 5's recycling principle from a single lesson's scope to the whole unit's.

v: 5 minutes at the start of each lesson
Cards or board prompts from the previous lesson

items: Start every lesson in the unit with five minutes on the previous lesson’s language.
Vary the format: a quick quiz, a chunk race, a picture prompt, a pair question.
In the middle of the unit, include language from two or three lessons back, not only the last one.
At the end of the unit, run a longer recycle covering the whole unit.
Note which items learners still find hard and include them in the next unit.
Learners design the recycle activity for the class.
Use a ‘memory box’ of cards drawn at random.
Support: include picture clues.
Stretch: learners must use recycled items in new sentences.

lines: Chunk race: call out opposite; pairs write a sentence using it.
Picture prompt: show a picture from a previous lesson; learners describe it.
Question circle: each learner asks the next one a question using the target structure.

body: Purpose: to show language returning across lessons. Content: five lesson boxes in a row. A coloured thread runs from lesson 1 back into lessons 2, 3 and 5; another thread from lesson 2 into lessons 3 and 4. The threads weave the lessons together. Style: simple, colourful threads. Board version: boxes joined by curved lines.

items: Wordwall or Quizlet (free basic versions). Quick recycle games reused across the unit.

blocks.x: A ‘memory box’ of cards with words and sentence starters from each lesson.

pts: Allocate more time early for input-heavy lessons, less for later output-heavy consolidation — or the reverse, depending on level and task.
Lower-level units often need more early input time; higher-level units can move to production faster.
Build pacing into the scheme explicitly rather than discovering the imbalance mid-unit.

items: Estimate how long each lesson needs for this class, not an average class.
For lower levels, give more time to input (listening, reading, presentation).
For higher levels, give more time to output (tasks, discussion, writing).
Mark one lesson as flexible: it can expand or shrink.
After the unit, compare planned and actual time and adjust for next time.
Plan two versions of the unit: a fast and a slow route through the same material.
Ask learners at the end of each lesson: too fast, right or too slow?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Pacing for two levels of the same unit:

lines: A1 class: 3 input lessons, 1 practice lesson, 1 short task lesson.
A2 class: 2 input lessons, 1 practice lesson, 2 task lessons (planning and presenting).

In the first, most segments are coloured blue (‘input’) with a small orange end (‘output’); in the second, blue shrinks and orange grows. Style: simple two-colour bars. Board version: not applicable.

pts: A brief progress check partway through a unit catches gaps before they surface in the final cumulative task.
Keep the checkpoint light — a quick task-based check, not a formal test that disrupts the unit's momentum.
Use checkpoint results to adjust the remaining lessons, not just to record a score.

v: A short task based on the unit aim

items: Midway through the unit, set a short task that previews the cumulative task (for example, each learner suggests one picnic place and gives a reason).
Listen or read quickly, using a simple checklist.
Sort learners into ‘on track’, ‘nearly’ and ‘needs support’.
Adjust the remaining lessons: more practice for a common gap, a support group, or an early extension.
Tell learners what you noticed and what will happen next.
Use a can-do self-assessment instead (Unit 2).
Use an exit ticket with a question that targets the unit aim.
Support: a sentence frame for the checkpoint task.
Stretch: ask for two reasons and a comparison.

lines: Most learners use Why don’t we…? confidently; few use going to. → Add ten minutes of going to practice in lesson 4.
Five learners cannot yet name places. → Give a picture word bank in the next lesson.

body: Purpose: to show a checkpoint midway. Content: a road leading to a flag (‘unit goal’). Halfway along, a small checkpoint booth with a clipboard. Three paths branch briefly from the booth and rejoin the road: ‘on track’, ‘nearly’, ‘needs support’. Style: friendly map illustration. Board version: not applicable.

items: Plickers (free basic version). A three-question check answered with cards and scanned by the teacher’s phone.

blocks.x: A class list with three columns ticked during a short speaking round.

body: For your next unit, run a halfway check and change one lesson because of it. At the end of the unit, compare results with the previous unit. The difference, even if small, shows what the checkpoint was worth.

dek: Unit 11 of 100: a single lesson teaches a point; a unit builds toward something bigger. This poster sequences several lessons around one cumulative communicative outcome.

aims.x: This unit moves from planning one lesson to planning a sequence of lessons. It shows how a unit of work can build towards a single communicative outcome, how language can return in spirals rather than appearing once, and how to check progress before the end.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain why a unit of work does more for learning than a series of separate lessons;
sequence a unit so that key language returns with increasing complexity;
write one unit-level aim and check each lesson against it;
balance the four skills across a unit;
design a cumulative task that draws on everything the unit taught;
recycle language across lessons, not only within them;
pace a unit to suit level and task;
run a light mid-unit checkpoint and act on it.

why: Why this matters. Units 1–10 built one strong lesson. But learners retain and transfer language across a sequence, not a single class — sequencing is where that retention is engineered.

background.x: A single lesson can teach a phrase. It rarely teaches a learner to use that phrase confidently, in different situations, weeks later. That needs repetition, variety and time, and those are properties of sequences rather than of single lessons. This is why most coursebooks are organized in units and why experienced teachers think in units even when their timetable shows only periods.

The idea of returning to the same content at increasing depth is often associated with Jerome Bruner, who proposed a spiral curriculum in which ‘any subject can be taught effectively in some intellectually honest form to any child at any stage of development’ and then revisited in more sophisticated forms (Bruner 1960: 33). Language teaching suits the spiral naturally. Learners meet going to for simple plans at A1, return to it for predictions at A2, and contrast it with will and the present continuous at B1.

A unit also gives lessons a shared destination. Kathleen Graves (2000) and I. S. P. Nation and John Macalister (2010) both describe course design as working backwards from goals to content and activities. At unit level, the goal is usually a single piece of communication that learners could not manage at the start: planning a school event, giving a short presentation, writing a complaint. Every lesson in the unit contributes something to it.

For teachers following a prescribed textbook, unit planning does not mean abandoning the book. It means reading a textbook unit as a whole before teaching its first lesson, deciding what it is building towards, and making sure the separate exercises actually add up.

items: Cumulative task rubric. Assess the final task against the unit aim with three criteria: task achieved, target language used, clarity.
Checkpoint comparison. Compare the proportion of learners ‘on track’ at the checkpoint with those who achieve the unit aim.
Recycling recall. At the end of the unit, test recall of language from the first lesson.
Learner self-assessment. Learners rate themselves against the unit aim before and after the unit.
Do you read a whole textbook unit before teaching it? What difference might it make?
Which language points return in your syllabus, and which appear only once?
What is the final task in the unit you are teaching now? Is it real communication?
How do you decide how long to spend on each lesson?
What happens in your classes when learners are behind at the middle of a unit?

terms.def: A final task at the end of a unit that draws on all the language and skills taught, such as a group presentation or campaign.
A planned point in a unit of work where the teacher checks learners’ progress, for example with a short task, and adjusts the rest of the unit in response.
Managing the speed and timing of lesson stages so that learners are neither rushed nor bored, and the lesson achieves its aim in the time available.

Planned reintroduction of previously taught language in new contexts and activities so that it is met, retrieved and used repeatedly over time. Recycling helps vocabulary and grammar move from recognition towards fluent, confident use.

The proportion of attention given to each of the four skills across a unit or course. Many textbook-led courses overemphasize reading and writing, so teachers plan to restore time for listening and speaking.

A curriculum in which topics and language are revisited repeatedly over time, each time at a greater level of depth or complexity (Bruner 1960). The past tense might be met first in simple stories, later in narratives and reports.
The overall goal of a unit of work, stating what learners should be able to do by its end. Each lesson aim should move learners closer to it.
A coherent block of lessons, usually over several weeks, built around a theme, text or outcome, with aims, a sequence of activities and assessment.
